newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Signs of hope emerge in Chechnya as truce holds.
newsitem.headline: Signs of hope emerge in Chechnya as truce holds.

text.p: Peace talks between Moscow and Chechen separatists are starting to bear fruit, despite stark predictions that last month's sacking of Russian peace envoy Alexander Lebed would provoke new fighting.

In the four weeks since President Boris Yeltsin fired the man who negotiated a deal which ended nearly 21 months of fighting, major clashes have been averted and Moscow's new peace envoys have made a flurry of trips to the rebel southern region.
Although Moscow and the separatists remain divided on many political issues and peace cannot be guaranteed, they say they are close to an agreement clarifying their relations.

In a change of tactics, Moscow is using economic levers more than ever to make remaining in Russia look more attractive to the separatists and rebel leaders have swapped their combat fatigues for business suits.

"What is extraordinary is the extremely low intensity of fighting. Despite the gloomy assessments when Lebed was sacked, the separatists seem to have their fighters under control," said Andrei Piontkovsky of Moscow's Centre for Strategic Studies.

Hopes of peace increased when Ivan Rybkin, Lebed's replacement, and separatist negotiators said on Tuesday they were close to an agreement defining their relations until January 27, when Chechnya is due to elect a regional leader and parliament.

In another hopeful sign, Moscow has raised no obstacles to the elections -- planned under the August 31 peace deal signed by Lebed -- even though the rebels set the date without consulting the Russian government.

The Kremlin has tacitly accepted the rebels' refusal to deal with Doku Zavgayav, whom it installed as head of the Chechnya administration, and recognised that the real power in the small North Caucasus region lies with the rebels.
Moscow has also has proposed making Chechnya a free economic zone, a move which would excuse the region from tax and duties.
The Russian government and the rebels have good reasons for lasting peace apart from the cost in human and financial terms.
More fighting would set back the separatists' hopes of rebuilding Chechnya, parts of which are already devastated, and could break their grip on the region.
Russian troops are in disarray after proving unable to crush the separatists in fighting which killed tens of thousands.

More fighting would make a long guerrilla war likely, hinder Yeltsin's ability to concentrate on economic and other problems when he returns to the Kremlin after heart surgery and boost Lebed's image as a peacemaker -- something Yeltsin would dread.
"The resumption of full-scale war would help make Lebed the next president of Russia," Piontkovsky said.
"There are still many problems but I think fighting can be ruled out this winter."
Yeltsin, who sacked Lebed on October 17 after accusing him of harbouring presidential ambitions and not working as part of a team, has replaced him with a loyal moderate in Rybkin.

The appointment of businessman Boris Berezovsky to join peace talks as Rybkin's deputy was more surprising, signalling an intention to use the lure of investment to persuade Chechnya to remain at least loosely tied to Russia.
"Berezovsky's role shows the future. He seems intent on 'buying' the separatist leaders," said Sergei Markov, an analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think-tank.
Berezovsky has already visited Chechnya and been to oil-rich Kazakhstan and neighbouring Georgia on trips which have fuelled speculation that Moscow is using oil to win over the separatists.

Lebed says Berezovksy has proposed that any new pipelines carrying Caspian region oil to world markets via Russia would run through Chechnya -- giving Moscow and Chechen leaders a share of the spoils.
Flowing oil would help revitalise Chechnya's oil-processing, its biggest and most proitable industry.
"If the pipeline goes to Novorossiysk, the rehabilitation of the Chechen economy is guaranteed in six months," Lebed said in an interview with the newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda on Monday.
Hinting that Berezovksy would also gain from the deal, Lebed said: "If the Chechens agree to the pipeline for the benefit of big business, Berezovsky will become the chief peacemaker."

Piontkovsky said widescale fighting could now be ruled out for the winter, but Markov said the failure to resolve the central problem of whether Chechnya should be in or out of Russia remained a major obstacle to permanent peace.
"They are looking for a way out but there are still serious contradictions between the two sides. I still believe it will take many years to solve this conflict," he said.
